1.title: Quality, Resources and Procurement
1.text: Welcome to Module 8. Quality, resources and procurement are the machinery that makes a plan deliverable: how good the work must be, who and what does it, and what you buy from outside. In Part 1, we start with quality: how to plan it, build it in, control it, and improve it. Part 2 covers resources and the start of procurement. Part 3 completes procurement, including contracts, negotiation and disputes.

1.title: Where This Module Sits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits. The Process domain has ten tasks, and this module covers three. Task seven: plan and optimize quality. Task four: plan and manage resources. Task five: plan and manage procurement. Quality questions reward prevention and early, continuous checks. Resource questions reward realistic capacity and following the right route. Procurement questions reward fairness and choosing the contract type that fits the risk.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. Plan quality requirements, metrics and tests, and build quality in. Tell assurance from control, read control charts and use the basic tools. Plan and acquire resources, optimize them and keep people well. Decide make or buy, select sources fairly and pick a contract type. Negotiate, manage suppliers and contracts, and handle claims. And manage the cost of quality and drive continuous improvement.

1.title: Case Check-In: Quality on the Microgrid
1.text: On the microgrid, quality is planned differently in each lane. The software lane uses a definition of done that includes tests, accessibility, security and documentation in every iteration. The hardware lane has a test and inspection plan for panels, batteries and switchgear, planned early. Grid-code and safety evidence is kept in a controlled, accessible repository, so auditors can find it. And independent audits check that the team follows the quality plan. Quality is built in, not inspected in at the end.

1.title: Quality: Key Terms
1.text: Key terms. Quality is the degree to which the inherent characteristics of a deliverable help meet or exceed the project's target objectives. Quality assurance uses project processes effectively and follows standards. Quality control creates deliverables that meet defined specifications and thresholds. A quality metric describes an attribute and how assurance will verify compliance. A specification is a required attribute, and tolerance is the acceptable variation. The definition of done lists the criteria for work to count as complete. And grade is not quality: low grade is not a problem, low quality is.

1.title: Quality Assurance Versus Quality Control
1.text: Quality assurance and quality control differ. Assurance focuses on processes and standards. It is preventive and builds confidence that future output will conform. Its tools are audits, checklists and process analysis, and in PMBOK 8 it lives in the Governance domain. Control focuses on deliverables and their specifications. It is detective: it finds nonconformance so it can be repaired. Its tools are inspection, testing and control charts, and it lives in Monitor and Control Scope. A memory aid: audit a process, inspect or test a product.

1.title: Gather Quality Requirements
1.text: Gather quality requirements from stakeholder expectations, the business case, contracts, regulations and standards, organizational policies and product attributes. Capture them as requirements, in the requirements documentation and the traceability matrix. Make them measurable and testable: if the goal is high quality, agree measurable outcomes first. Identify them in Define Scope, including how compliance will be demonstrated. Regulatory requirements and customer-required sustainability criteria are quality requirements. In agile work, use acceptance criteria and a definition of done.

1.title: The Quality Management Plan
1.text: The quality management plan describes how the organization's policies and procedures will be applied to reach quality objectives. It may include quality standards and quality objectives. It covers roles and responsibilities, and the deliverables and processes subject to review. It covers planned quality assurance and control activities, tools and methodologies, and procedures for nonconformance and continuous improvement. Plan quality metrics and the way assurance will verify them. Review the plan early, so decisions use accurate information, with a sharper focus on value and less rework.

1.title: Plan Tests and Inspections
1.text: Plan test and inspection activities: how each product or deliverable will be tested or inspected to meet stakeholder needs and performance and reliability goals. Tests depend on the industry, such as unit and regression tests in software, strength and soil tests in construction, and stress screening in hardware. Specifications without verification methods leave a gap. Put quality activities into the schedule, budget and resources, and do quality work as early as possible, which people call shifting left. Prevention comes first: training, documented processes, checklists and a definition of ready.

1.title: Manage Quality Assurance
1.text: Manage Quality Assurance turns the plan into executable activities that follow standards and policies. A quality audit is a structured, independent process, usually by a team outside the project, scheduled or random. Its aim is to find good practices, nonconformities and gaps, share good practices and offer help positively. Checklists come from history and lessons learned, and are never exhaustive. Process analysis finds non-value-added steps. Outputs are a quality report and change requests. Audit findings that change an approved process go through change control.

1.title: Quality Control: Inspect, Test, Measure
1.text: Quality control happens inside Monitor and Control Scope, using data from the work. Inspection examines a work product to see whether it conforms to documented standards, and it also verifies defect repairs. Testing is an organized investigation to find errors, defects and nonconformance, and early testing finds problems sooner and cheaper. Use variance, trend and root cause analysis. Use statistical sampling when testing every unit is costly or destructive. Results are quality control measurements and verified deliverables. Then the customer validates.

1.title: Control Charts
1.text: A control chart shows whether a process is stable and predictable. It has a mean and control limits, calculated from the process data, usually plus or minus three standard deviations. Special-cause signals include a point outside the control limits. They include about seven consecutive points on one side of the mean, the rule of seven. And they include a run of points trending in one direction. Investigate the assignable cause even if every point is inside the limits. And do not adjust a stable process because of normal variation. The rule of seven and the three-sigma limits are exam practice. PMBOK 8 describes control charts without numeric rules.

1.title: Control Limits Versus Specification Limits
1.text: Control limits and specification limits are different. Specification limits come from the requirements. Control limits come from the process's own data, using standard statistical methods. A process can be in control and still fail the specification, because it is stable but centered in the wrong place. A process inside the specification can still be out of control, and so unpredictable. For normal data, plus or minus one standard deviation covers about sixty-eight percent, two about ninety-five, and three about ninety-nine point seven. Six Sigma is about three point four defects per million.

1.title: The Basic Quality Tools
1.text: Know the basic quality tools. The cause-and-effect diagram, or fishbone, traces an effect to root causes. A flowchart maps steps, decisions and handoffs, and finds weak points and waste. A checklist or check sheet reminds and tallies defects by type. A histogram shows the distribution of data. A Pareto chart ranks causes by frequency so you fix the vital few first. A scatter diagram shows correlation, which is not proof of cause. An affinity diagram groups ideas. Root cause analysis finds the underlying reason, and removing it stops recurrence. Pareto analysis is exam practice.

1.title: Pareto Analysis
1.text: Here is a Pareto chart of defect causes on a hardware deliverable. Causes are ranked by frequency, with a cumulative line. Two causes, wiring and labels, produce most of the defects. That is the vital few: the eighty-twenty idea. So start there. Do not spread effort evenly across all causes. Then find the root cause of the top items, fix it, and verify that the fix worked. Pareto is exam practice. PMBOK 8 lists the other basic tools.

1.title: Ongoing Quality Reviews
1.text: Reviews should run throughout each phase, not only at phase gates, because defects accumulate between infrequent reviews and deeper end-of-phase reviews still find them late. Review types include peer reviews, design and code reviews, and inspections. They include test results, gate reviews and quality audits. And they include sprint reviews, retrospectives, and definition-of-done checks in every iteration. Make results visible in quality reports and dashboards, agree actions, and feed findings back into the plan and the process.

1.title: Quality in Agile Work
1.text: In agile work, quality is built in through the definition of done: automated tests, accessibility, security, documentation and compliance. Acceptance criteria sit on each story, and are updated as the product evolves. Test inside the iteration. A separate testing phase at the end finds defects late and delays release. Compliance checks, such as accessibility, belong in every iteration's definition of done, not in a final audit. Agree the definition of done with the team and the product owner, not unilaterally.

1.title: Compliance, Cost of Quality and Sustainability
1.text: Regulatory and standards requirements are quality requirements: confirm which apply, classify them, and put them into the quality plan and acceptance criteria. Plan verification methods that demonstrate compliance, and keep evidence in a controlled, accessible repository so auditors can find it. Build compliance checks into the definition of done or phase exit criteria. Sustainability is a quality dimension: poor quality wastes materials, energy and travel, so prevention reduces environmental cost. Put sustainability criteria into quality requirements and the definition of done. Reassess when regulations change.

1.title: Cost of Quality
1.text: Cost of quality has two sides. Conformance costs, prevention and appraisal, rise as you invest more. Nonconformance costs, internal failure such as rework and external failure such as warranty claims, fall as you invest more. The total has a minimum: the optimal cost of quality, where extra prevention and appraisal stop paying off. Prevention costs less than appraisal and failure. More inspection alone does not fix a process that creates defects. Include the cost of quality in estimates and the budget, and track failure costs as a sign that quality planning is weak.

1.title: Continuous Improvement
1.text: PMBOK 8 names several continuous improvement approaches: plan-do-check-act, Lean, Total Quality Management, Six Sigma and the five focusing steps from the theory of constraints. With plan-do-check-act, plan the change. Do it on a small scale. Check the results against the target. And act: standardize if it worked, otherwise adjust and repeat. Standardize what works by updating checklists and process assets. Retrospectives are the team-level engine: commit to a few improvements and track them. Inspect and adapt the improvement process itself.

1.title: Quality in Predictive, Agile and Hybrid Work
1.text: Quality differs by approach. Predictive: a quality management plan up front, with metrics, audits and a test plan. Inspections and tests at defined points. Ongoing peer reviews plus gate reviews. And acceptance against criteria. Agile: acceptance criteria and a definition of done, continuous testing inside each iteration, sprint reviews with feedback time, and a retrospective every iteration. Hybrid: a plan for the fixed or regulated parts, a definition of done for the iterative parts, gates for the envelope and sprint reviews inside.

1.title: Quality Traps: What PMI Expects
1.text: The traps for quality. Assurance is about process and control is about product. Prevention beats inspection: when defects keep occurring, fix the process rather than adding inspections. Build quality in: put tests and compliance in the definition of done, and test early. Reviews are ongoing. Rule of seven: investigate a special cause, and remember that control limits are not specification limits. Audits are independent and constructive. Quality problems create change requests. And do not gold-plate: extra features are not quality.

1.title: Part 1 Recap
1.text: Let us recap Part 1. Quality requirements are measurable, with verification methods and metrics, and quality work starts early. Assurance audits the process, and control inspects and tests the product. Know the rule of seven, the difference between control and specification limits, Pareto analysis and root cause analysis. Reviews are ongoing, with a definition of done in every iteration. Prevention is the cheapest part of the cost of quality. And improvement uses plan-do-check-act, with a few tracked actions. In Part 2, we turn to resources.

2.title: Resources: Key Terms
2.text: Part 2 covers resources. Key terms. A resource manager has management authority over resources, such as a functional manager. Resources include people and also physical, material or virtual resources: equipment, materials, facilities, software, licenses and test environments. A role is the function, a responsibility is the duty, authority is the right to decide and apply resources, and competence is skill and capacity. Authority should match responsibility. A resource breakdown structure lists resources by category and type, and a resource calendar shows when each is available.

2.title: The Five Resource Processes
2.text: Five resource processes. Plan Resource Management produces the resource management plan and the team charter. Estimate Resources produces resource requirements and a resource breakdown structure. Acquire Resources produces resource and team assignments. Lead the Team guides, develops and manages the team, and produces team performance assessments. Monitor and Control Resourcing makes sure physical and virtual resources are available as planned, compares planned with actual use, and releases them when done. The aim: the right resources, in the right place, at the right time and amount.

2.title: Plan Resource Management
2.text: The resource management plan describes how resources are identified, acquired, allocated, monitored and controlled. It covers how to identify and quantify team and physical resources. It covers how to acquire them, including the sourcing route, such as the PMO pool. And it covers roles with their authority, responsibility and competence, and what to do about gaps. It includes organization charts, how team members are released, training and team development. It includes resource control for inventory, equipment and supplies, and a recognition plan.

2.title: RACI and Hierarchical Charts
2.text: The responsibility assignment matrix links work packages or activities to resources, showing all the work of one person and all the people on one activity. Only one person is accountable per task. RACI, responsible, accountable, consulted and informed, is a common form. Hierarchical charts include the organizational breakdown structure of units that do the work, the work breakdown structure of deliverables, the resource breakdown structure, and the value breakdown structure. Text-oriented formats, such as position descriptions, spell out responsibilities, authority and competencies.

2.title: Team Charter and Skill Matrix
2.text: The team charter records the team's values, communication guidelines, decision-making, conflict resolution, meeting guidelines and agreements. It works best when the team creates it, and it should be revisited when new members join, so they help shape the ground rules. The skill matrix compares required and available skills and exposes gaps. Green human resource management uses people practices that favor sustainable use of resources. The resource-based view identifies strategic resources, tested with value, rarity, imitability and organization.

2.title: Estimate Resources
2.text: Estimate resources for each work package or activity: the type, quantity and characteristics of people, and of physical or virtual resources. Equipment, materials, test environments and licenses must be estimated with the labor, including lead times, not as an afterthought. Align resource, cost and duration estimates. Techniques include expert judgment, bottom-up, analogous and parametric estimating, and alternative analysis. Outputs are resource requirements with assumptions about availability, a basis of estimates and a resource breakdown structure. The benefit is anticipating shortages and surpluses.

2.title: A Resource Breakdown Structure
2.text: Here is a resource breakdown structure for the microgrid. Labor covers engineers, developers and electricians. Materials cover panels, batteries and cable. Equipment covers cranes and test rigs. Virtual resources cover licenses and test environments. The structure groups resources by category, and by type, such as skill level, grade or certification. It helps you estimate each category, spot shortages, and plan lead times. Remember that equipment, materials and environments are estimated together with the labor.

2.title: Acquire Resources
2.text: Acquire Resources obtains and assigns the team and physical or virtual resources. Collaborate, negotiate and influence the people who can provide them, such as functional managers, suppliers and partners. Follow the sourcing route in the resource management plan, rather than bypassing it. Use actual availability from resource calendars, especially for preassigned resources. If a resource is not available, an alternative is possible, within limits. Failing to acquire resources raises risk, and in the worst case can cancel the project.

2.title: When a Resource Is Not Available
2.text: Suppose a needed resource is not available because of economic factors or assignment to other projects. You may assign an alternative with different competencies, features or cost, but only if the risks are acknowledged and legal, regulatory or mandatory criteria are not violated. Document the effect on schedule, budget, risks, quality and training plans. Never skip a mandatory qualification to save time. If a resource is available only part-time, remember that agile teams work best with dedicated, cross-functional members.

2.title: Virtual Teams and Colocation
2.text: Virtual teams widen the talent pool: distributed locations, shifts, home offices, and no travel cost. But they need more planning of communication, clear expectations, conflict protocols and cultural understanding. Provide collaboration sites, audio and video, ongoing messaging, and time to get to know remote members. Hold at least one face-to-face meeting where possible. Colocation, temporary or full, improves communication and productivity, with a team room and visible schedules. A new virtual team needs deliberate setup, starting with a team charter.

2.title: Optimizing Resource Needs
2.text: A resource histogram shows demand against capacity week by week. In weeks four to six, demand exceeds capacity: over-allocation. If the activities are not critical, use resource smoothing within float, so the end date is unchanged. Leveling may move the end date. If the over-allocation is on the critical path, leveling may delay the finish. So evaluate adding capacity, reassigning, resequencing or reducing scope. Use cost and risk analysis, and change control. Release resources on time when they are no longer needed.

2.title: Resource Situations and Responses
2.text: Common resource situations. A skill gap: use the skill matrix and choose training, coaching, mentoring, hiring or contracting by time, cost and risk. Competing demand from other projects: negotiate with the resource owners, and escalate through governance. A resource idle or no longer needed: release it on time. Agile capacity changes: plan iterations on actual capacity, and do not squeeze the team. Signs of burnout, such as minimum effort or silence in meetings: adjust the plan and support well-being. And consider sustainability across the value chain.

2.title: Monitor and Control Resourcing
2.text: Monitor and Control Resourcing is concerned with physical and virtual resources, and runs continuously. Monitor expenditures and planned versus actual use. Identify and deal with shortages and surpluses in good time. Make sure resources are used and released per plan. Inform stakeholders of resource issues and manage changes as they occur. Utilization indicators include actual against planned use, downtime against planned time, units produced against hours worked, and materials used, scrap and rework. Too much inventory raises cost, and too little blocks delivery.

2.title: Case Check-In: Resources for the Microgrid
2.text: Back to our microgrid. Specialized roles come through the PMO pool, not around it. The software team is dedicated and cross-functional, and iterations are planned on actual capacity. Cranes and test rigs are estimated with the labor, including lead times. During the cut-over, watch workload and well-being: if the team shows burnout signs, adjust the plan and capacity, not just overtime. And release equipment and people on time when their work ends, so idle resources do not cost money.

2.title: Resources in Predictive, Agile and Hybrid Work
2.text: Resources differ by approach. Predictive: allocation defined early from the schedule, and a detailed resource management plan. Functional or matrix structures with formal roles. Centralized leadership. And leveling and smoothing. Agile: self-organizing, collaborative teams, dedicated and cross-functional, often three to nine members. Distributed or servant leadership. Capacity-based iteration planning. And control through velocity and impediment removal. Hybrid: predictive for fixed or specialist resources, adaptive teams for variable work.

2.title: Resource Traps: What PMI Expects
2.text: The traps for resources. Resources are people and things, so estimate equipment, materials and environments with the labor. One accountable person per activity. Follow the sourcing route, and use alternatives only within legal limits, with documented impact. Authority must match responsibility: negotiate with managers, and escalate if they cannot agree. Smooth within float first, and plan agile iterations on actual capacity. Release idle resources, watch well-being, and co-create the team charter, revisiting it when members join.

2.title: Procurement: Key Terms
2.text: Now procurement. Key terms. Procurement is acquiring goods, services or results from external sources. The buyer purchases, and the seller, vendor, contractor or supplier, provides. An agreement is any document that defines initial intentions: a contract, purchase order, service-level agreement, memorandum of understanding or letter of agreement. The statement of work describes what is purchased. The sourcing strategy plan records what is insourced or outsourced. Source selection uses predefined weighted criteria. A claim is a request for relief under the agreement, and alternative dispute resolution settles disputes.

2.title: The Procurement Flow
2.text: Procurement has three stages. Plan: identify needs, involve key stakeholders early, analyze whether to buy, set procurement rules, identify potential sellers and prepare procurement documents. Conduct: obtain responses, evaluate, select, negotiate and award. The process must be transparent and fair, with equal opportunity for all potential sellers and bidder questions answered adequately and to everyone. Monitor, control and close: manage relationships, monitor contract performance, make changes, and close the contracts, confirming all obligations were met. The people authorized to procure may be team members, management or the purchasing department.

2.title: Plan Sourcing Strategy
2.text: Plan Sourcing Strategy documents sourcing decisions, specifies the source selection approach, defines the scope of work for external sourcing, and chooses appropriate contracts and sources. Include procurement and legal in the planning. It is different from resource planning: sourcing is about outsourcing work and deliverables. Tools include market research, make-or-buy analysis and source selection analysis. The output is the sourcing strategy plan, with insourcing and outsourcing decisions and the selection criteria.

2.title: Make or Buy
2.text: Make-or-buy compares insourcing with outsourcing. Insourcing uses internal expertise, is often cheaper when much innovation is needed, integrates tightly with strategic advantage, and gives more control. Outsourcing uses external expertise when missing internally, is often cheaper when the goods or services are common, frees capacity and capital, and transfers delivery risk to the supplier. Weigh current allocation, skills, the need for specialized or independent expertise, and the wish to avoid permanent employment obligations. The analysis may use payback, return on investment or net present value.

2.title: The Procurement Management Plan
2.text: The procurement management plan describes how the team acquires goods and services from outside. It covers coordination with the schedule, a timetable and metrics, roles and the team's authority when a procurement department exists, and constraints and assumptions. It covers the legal jurisdiction and payment currency, and the bidding approach. It covers whether independent estimates are used. It covers risk measures, such as performance bonds or insurance, and any prequalified sellers. The procurement strategy then decides the delivery method, the type of binding agreement and the phases.

2.title: Part 2 Recap
2.text: Let us recap Part 2. Plan and estimate resources using the sourcing route and a resource breakdown structure, with equipment and materials estimated with the labor. Acquire by negotiating, using real availability, and using alternatives only within legal limits. Set up teams with a charter, deliberate virtual arrangements and capacity-based planning. Optimize by smoothing within float, releasing idle resources and watching well-being. Control by comparing planned with actual use. And procurement starts with its terms, three stages and a fair process, then sourcing strategy, make or buy, and the procurement plan. In Part 3, we complete procurement: strategy, selection, contracts and disputes.

3.title: Procurement Strategy and Delivery Methods
3.text: The procurement strategy decides the delivery method, the type of legally binding agreement, and how procurement advances through phases. For professional services: buyer and provider with or without subcontracting, a joint venture, or a provider acting as the buyer's representative. For build-out supply: turnkey, design-build, design-bid-build and build-own-operate-transfer. Integrated project delivery uses one multiparty agreement with shared risk and reward and open-book accounting. Define procurement phases with objectives, indicators, criteria for moving on, and knowledge transfer.

3.title: Develop a Delivery Solution
3.text: Choose how the need will actually be met: build, buy, lease, adapt or partner. Compare options with alternative analysis, multicriteria decision analysis and cost-benefit analysis, and favor options that deliver value early and reduce risk. For example, an off-the-shelf product meets about eighty percent of the need, and a custom build would take a year. Then buy now, and close the gap in later increments. This is exam practice. The point is to avoid one big, irreversible bet.

3.title: Bid Documents
3.text: Four bid documents. A request for information gathers market information before sending bid documents to selected vendors. A request for proposal suits complex or complicated scope where the buyer wants the vendor to propose a solution. A request for quote suits purchases where price is the main factor and the solution is readily available. An invitation for bid, or invitation to tender, is a formal call for bids, evaluated mostly on price against a defined specification. At the bidder conference, give the same information to all bidders.

3.title: Source Selection Methods
3.text: PMBOK 8 names selection methods. Least cost suits standard, low-risk purchases. Qualifications only suits small purchases. Quality-based selection awards to the highest technical proposal score. Quality and cost based selection balances both. Single source applies when only one qualified seller exists, or an existing partner is used. Fixed budget gives the best value within a set budget. Review the priorities of the competing demands before choosing, and publish the evaluation method in the tender documents, so bidders know how they will be judged.

3.title: Weighted Scoring and Mandatory Minimums
3.text: Score each criterion, weight it by importance, and rank proposals by weighted total. The ranking sets the negotiation sequence. Typical criteria include capability and capacity, product and life cycle cost, and delivery dates. They include technical approach, experience and past performance, key staff, and financial strength. In this example, bidder B scores seven point five and bidder C seven point four. But there is a mandatory minimum technical score of seven, and bidder C scores six, so C is disqualified. Apply the minimum first, then rank the rest.

3.title: A Fair Selection Process
3.text: Fairness is central. Give equal information to all bidders, with the same answers to questions. Follow the published criteria, including past performance. Follow the organization's gift and conflict-of-interest policy. Never steer the award to a favored provider. If you have a relationship with a bidder, disclose it and step back. And keep records of evaluations. If a bidder offers a lavish gift during evaluation, decline it and handle it under policy. It must not influence the decision.

3.title: Contract Types and Cost Risk
3.text: Contract types shift cost risk. Fixed price: a predetermined fee for a clearly defined scope. The seller bears the cost risk, and the buyer gets budget certainty, perhaps with a risk premium. Cost-reimbursable: the seller's actual costs plus a fee, used when scope is uncertain or risk is high. The buyer bears the cost escalation risk. Time and materials: actual time and materials plus a margin, a hybrid for smaller projects, maintenance or unclear scope. Target cost: a target with sharing of savings and overruns, encouraging cost control.

3.title: Choosing the Contract Type
3.text: Choose the contract type by the situation. Clear, stable scope and a buyer who wants certainty: fixed price. Uncertain scope or high risk, such as research or complex construction: cost-reimbursable, with cost controls. Scope still evolving but exposure must be capped: time and materials with a not-to-exceed value. A wish to share efficiency gains: target cost or incentive terms. Agile, collaborative or outcome-based work: agile or collaborative contracts, with iteration-based deliverables, caps and incentives. Think from both sides, and structure contracts so they benefit all parties.

3.title: Emerging Contracting Practices
3.text: PMBOK 8 describes emerging practices. Agile or collaborative contracts: shared risk and reward, caps, reduced rates and performance incentives. Outcome-based contracts pay for results, so tie payments to validated results when you need to learn before committing. Sustainable contracting embeds environmental, social and governance principles in contracts, with measurable outcomes. Smart contracts, for example on blockchain, can pay on milestones. AI tools help analyze contracts, assess risk and predict overruns, but a human validates. Alignment with sustainability goals can also be a source selection criterion.

3.title: Negotiation
3.text: Negotiation clarifies the structure, rights and obligations so both parties agree before signing. Almost everything is negotiable: cost, delivery and payment dates, location of work, intellectual property. A procurement team member with authority to sign leads, and the project manager supports. Strategy: clarify your priorities and alternatives. Understand the other side's interests, not only positions. Use facts. Look for options that serve both parties, such as payments tied to milestones. Do not waive rights. And match the approach to the context.

3.title: Case Check-In: Procurement on the Microgrid
3.text: Procurement on our microgrid fits the contract to the risk. Panels and batteries have a well-defined scope, so use fixed price with the suppliers. The dashboard has an evolving scope, so use time and materials by iteration, with a cap and outcome incentives. Select suppliers on published weighted criteria, including sustainability and a mandatory technical minimum. Control changes by signed amendment, and remember that a free upgrade still needs impact assessment. A procurement team member with authority leads the negotiation.

3.title: Manage Suppliers and Contracts
3.text: Managing suppliers and contracts. Monitor performance against the contract, using regular and milestone status updates, reviews and walkthroughs. Inspect and accept deliverables against acceptance criteria. Handle a miss under the contract terms: notify the vendor formally, require correction, and withhold acceptance as the contract allows. Do not fix it quietly yourself, and do not accept it. Control changes through formal change control and a signed amendment, even for a free upgrade. Clarify who directs whose people. A procurement audit reviews contracts and processes. Evaluate vendor performance and keep records. Verify the objectives of the agreement were met, then close all contracts before the project is closed.

3.title: Claims and Disputes
3.text: Disputes rise with complexity and the number of stakeholders. Variation orders and time and cost overruns are leading causes of claims. PMBOK 8 lists alternative dispute resolution methods: negotiation, mediation, arbitration, dispute review boards, expert determination, and litigation as the last resort. As a project manager, understand the contract terms, keep detailed records, communicate openly, spot conflict early, and work with legal. Be careful with written language, since email can become evidence. Set escalation protocols, protect confidentiality, and stay impartial and factual.

3.title: Procurement in Predictive, Agile and Hybrid Work
3.text: Procurement differs by approach. Predictive: a detailed statement of work before bidding, fixed price for well-defined work, cost-reimbursable for uncertain work, and milestone acceptance. Change goes through formal contract change orders, and vendors report to the project manager. Agile: evolving requirements, and agile or collaborative contracts such as time and materials by iteration, with caps and incentives. Acceptance is per increment, and vendor staff work in the team. Hybrid mixes both.

3.title: Procurement Traps: What PMI Expects
3.text: The traps for procurement. Make or buy first, and compare options with analysis. Run a fair process: equal information, published criteria, no favoritism. Match the contract to the risk: fixed price for clear scope, cost-reimbursable for uncertain scope. A mandatory minimum disqualifies a bidder even with a top weighted score. Changes need a signed amendment, and free upgrades need impact assessment. Close all contracts before the project, after verifying that obligations were met. For disputes, negotiate first and escalate by protocol.

3.title: Module Recap
3.text: Let us recap the whole module. Quality: prevention, continuous checks, charts and tools, and the definition of done. Resources: people and things, real availability, the sourcing route, and well-being. Procurement: make or buy first, fair selection, and a contract that fits the risk. Control: audits, planned against actual use, and supplier performance. Improvement: a few tracked actions, and standardize what works. Now it is time to test yourself. Five questions follow. For each one, pause the video, choose your answer, and then listen to the explanation.

3.title: Practice Question 1
3.text: Question one. The same wiring defect keeps appearing in finished units, and the team proposes adding another inspection step at the end of the line. What should the project manager do? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is D. Prevention costs less than finding defects, so the project manager finds the root cause and improves the process. More inspection alone does not fix a process that creates defects. More inspection treats the symptom, slowing down is not an analysis, and replacing a supplier before analysis is a guess.

3.title: Practice Question 2
3.text: Question two. On a control chart, seven consecutive measurements fall above the mean, but all of them are inside the control limits. What should the project manager do? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is B. Seven consecutive points on one side of the mean signal a special cause even inside the control limits, so the project manager investigates the cause. Ignoring it, widening the limits, or adjusting a stable process without cause all miss the signal.

3.title: Practice Question 3
3.text: Question three. A team planned its iterations assuming five full-time members, but two were moved to operations support. The product owner still expects the same scope each iteration. What should the project manager do? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is C. Agile iterations are planned on actual available capacity, with the fixed team and flexible scope, agreed with the product owner. Overtime, hiding the shortfall, or demanding the members back without discussion ignore actual capacity.

3.title: Practice Question 4
3.text: Question four. A research-based development effort has an uncertain scope and high risk, and the buyer wants to keep flexibility. Which contract type fits best? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is A. Uncertain scope and high risk call for a cost-reimbursable contract with cost controls, because a fixed price would push risk onto a seller who cannot estimate it. Fixed price needs a defined scope, and uncapped time and materials leaves the buyer's exposure open.

3.title: Practice Question 5
3.text: Question five. In a tender, one bidder has the highest weighted score but falls below the mandatory minimum technical score. What should the project manager do? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is B. A mandatory minimum is applied first, so a bidder below it is disqualified even with the highest weighted total, and the others are ranked. Awarding anyway, changing the published rule, or letting one bidder resubmit are all unfair.

3.title: Answers at a Glance
3.text: Here are all five answers together. Question one: D. Find the root cause and prevent the defect instead of inspecting more. Question two: B. A run of seven on one side of the mean signals a special cause. Question three: C. Plan iterations on actual capacity and agree the scope. Question four: A. Uncertain scope and high risk call for cost-reimbursable with controls. Question five: B. A bidder below a mandatory minimum is disqualified before ranking. That completes Module 8. Next, Module 9 covers managing execution, status and metrics, and closure. See you there.
